extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of The Spectator; general educated public and essayists interested in moral and humorous writing
extracted.subtask_description: Producing short periodical essays that blend wit and moral instruction for an educated early-18th-century readership, balancing amusement with ethical reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-nature: steadiness and uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: First test of Good-Nature: whether it acts with steadiness and uniformity in sickness and in health, in prosperity and in adversity; if otherwise, it is only a transient humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transient, situational kindness (e.g., only petitioning a great man before dinner when he is in good humour) is not real moral Good-Nature. Evaluate by consistency across changing circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-nature: operates according to reason and duty (discrimination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Second test: whether benevolence makes distinctions between its objects and follows rules of reason and duty — not exerted promiscuously toward deserving and undeserving alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True Good-Nature should distinguish deserving recipients (not relieve the idle indiscriminately). If charity or kindness is given at random or by accident rather than choice, it is amiable instinct but not a moral virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-nature: willingness to suffer for others
rubrics_metrics.description: Third test: whether one is able to exert Good-Nature to one’s own disadvantage — willing to risk part of fortune, reputation, health, or ease for the benefit of mankind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured by readiness to endure pain, want, or inconvenience for others; charity (relieving the indigent) is singled out as a frequent practical test of this willingness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charity: proportionate provision and prudence
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule: those with more than sufficient competency should set aside a certain proportion of income for the poor, managing charity so as not to hurt one’s own family or friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical prescription (example of Eugenius): appropriate and regular allocation (e.g., a tenth), occasional voluntary additions, and prudence to ensure family is not prejudiced. The charity should be sustainable and not cause personal ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudent charitable practice (concrete methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of how to be generous without impoverishing oneself: fix particular days of fasting/abstinence to augment charity funds; redirect entertainment expenses to giving; make small habitual donations in place of minor conveniences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific behaviors: walk instead of coach and give the saved fare; give an evening’s theatre money to a needy person and accept simpler amusements instead. Aim to 'be generous, without impoverishing himself, and enjoy his Estate by making it the Property of others.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor writing: balance mercurial and saturnine readers
rubrics_metrics.description: The author should accommodate two general reader types — the mercurial (who desire wit and humour) and the saturnine (who seek moral and serious reflection) — by varying content rather than writing solely to one taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate entertainments of both kinds so that the sprightly reader may be led into profitable thought and the thoughtful reader may be pleasantly diverted; avoid always being grave or always being merry to retain a broad readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utile dulci: mix instruction with delight
rubrics_metrics.description: A good paper should 'mix utile dulci' — combining the useful (instruction/moral) with the sweet (pleasure/humour) to both delight and admonish the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to make readers insensibly engaged in serious thinking while they expect mere diversion. The mixture of entertainment and instruction increases usefulness and reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor ethics: avoid immorality and ill-nature in wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour should be kept innocent and free from ill-nature; the discreet author suppresses many strokes of raillery or glances of ill-nature that would corrupt minds or injure reputations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise modesty and restraint: stifle tempting lines that have remote tendency to corrupt, avoid personal malignity, and omit raillery that would unjustly harm others. The author aims to be diverting without being immoral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit without licentious liberties requires genius
rubrics_metrics.description: It is easy to be a wit with liberties that offend; it requires genius and invention to appear witty without resorting to immoral or ill-natured freedoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality humour is marked by clever suppression and invention: the author must find ways to be amusing that do not rely on degrading or corrupting content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjugal conduct: husbands should be regular and agreeable at home
rubrics_metrics.description: Husbands are admonished to keep a more regular and civil behaviour towards their wives; being least agreeable where most obliged is a wrong that inflicts exquisite torments on those who love them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical counsel: avoid returning from outings with a 'gaol-like' manner, refrain from moodiness that causes jealousy, and maintain kindness and temperate conduct in private as part of conjugal morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public amusements and contests: composure under provocation
rubrics_metrics.description: In skill-based entertainments (e.g., whistling competitions), success is judged by composure — e.g., whistling clearest and completing a tune without laughing while provoked by antics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitions reward steadiness of countenance and resistance to provocation (the winning whistler maintained settled countenance and resisted the Merry-Andrew’s tricks). Similar principles apply to other playful contests (e.g., yawning contests judged by naturalness and inducement of yawns).
